strengths: The manuscript :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/iclr2026--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-6fi1etbl/call-0ef6bc8cfc644b938fa61d2d4a787a82/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"} addresses the important problem of long-horizon memory in offline RL. Combining segment recurrence, memory tokens, cached states, and cross-attention is intuitive and practically relevant.

The evaluation spans several memory-oriented domains, including T-Maze, ViZDoom-Two-Colors, Memory Maze, Minigrid-Memory, and POPGym, plus Atari and MuJoCo. It includes transformer, recurrent, value-based, and state-space baselines.

The long-horizon T-Maze extrapolation is a useful diagnostic: RATE retains a one-bit cue far beyond its training horizon, while several context-limited baselines collapse. The comparisons among multiple MRV variants also provide some evidence that the exact update mechanism matters.

The appendix reports many useful implementation details, including encoders, RATE hyperparameters, run counts, hardware, parameter counts, and efficiency measurements; code is also reportedly supplied.
weaknesses: The central preservation theorem is invalid as written. The alignment assumption gives, for each old memory row, the existence of some aligned value row, whereas the pigeonhole argument gives a potentially different index whose attention weight is at least 1/m; the proof simply equates these indices. It also discards potentially negative contributions from all other value rows and assumes the output memory row is unit-normalized although only the input row was assumed normalized.

Even if those proof errors were repaired, the stated lower bound is vacuous for every reported configuration: with m between 5 and 30 and alpha at most 1, the multiplier 1-sqrt(2(1-alpha/m)) is negative. Moreover, preserving vector norm is not equivalent to preserving task-relevant information, and a one-update norm bound would not establish long-horizon retention. Thus the abstract and conclusion's theoretical guarantee is unsupported.

The MRV is not clearly a retention gate: old memory appears only as the query, while the output is formed entirely from transformed new values, with no residual path from old memory. It cannot recover information already absent from those values. The method otherwise largely combines established RMT-style memory tokens and Transformer-XL caching, making the incremental novelty modest.

The ablations do not establish that the three advertised mechanisms are complementary. The main component evidence uses inference-time noise, which creates an out-of-distribution perturbation rather than measuring models trained without each component. MRV variants are evaluated mainly on synthetic T-Maze; Table 8 indicates that T-Maze uses no cached states and Memory Maze uses zero MRV heads, so the full combination is not what drives several headline results.

Baseline coverage and tuning fairness are inadequate for the strongest claims. The POPGym aggregate compares RATE only with DT and basic behavior-cloning models, omitting RMT, Transformer-XL, state-space models, and relevant memory architectures such as FFM and SHM. RATE is heavily tuned by domain, but comparable baseline configurations, search spaces, and tuning budgets are not reported.

The statistical evidence is weak. Most memory experiments use only three or four independent training runs; it is unclear whether SEM is computed across runs or pooled over the 100 evaluation episodes. There are no confidence intervals or hypothesis tests supporting repeated claims of significant improvement, despite many environments, configurations, and small numerical differences.

The general-purpose and state-of-the-art claims are overstated. On MuJoCo, RATE's average score of 78.5 is below several reported competitors, and Table 3 shows it as best on only 2 of 9 tasks despite the text claiming 3 of 9. Atari covers only four games. These comparisons also mix newly obtained results with numbers from prior papers, while RATE receives a custom per-segment return-to-go reset that is neither properly ablated nor applied to the compared methods.

Several protocol inconsistencies impede interpretation and reproduction: POPGym is variously described as having 46 and 48 tasks, and its reported 'average' aggregates appear to be sums; ViZDoom descriptions disagree about trajectory length and when the pillar disappears; the POPGym dataset size and baseline contexts are unspecified; Equation 3 includes an FFN absent from Algorithm 2; and the algorithm does not specify cached-state integration, memory-gradient truncation, positional encoding, or inference-state handling. Some appendix figures are also too small to read reliably.

The headline extrapolation task is narrow and confounded. T-Maze requires retaining only one bit, supplies an explicit pre-junction flag, and uses successful oracle trajectories dominated by repeated straight actions. The authors themselves observe terminal-action class imbalance, so baseline failures can reflect optimization and loss weighting rather than memory capacity. Stronger balanced-loss controls and less synthetic long-horizon tasks are needed.

strengths: The paper addresses an important problem—long-horizon memory in offline RL—and presents the recurrent segmentation and memory-token architecture clearly. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/iclr2026--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-2y75mwou/call-517521ac8ba344a39979fb5cca71c87b/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}

The empirical scope is unusually broad, covering synthetic recall tasks, visual POMDPs, POPGym, Atari, and MuJoCo, with transformer, recurrent, state-space, behavior-cloning, and offline-RL baselines.

The T-Maze results provide compelling evidence that RATE can propagate a one-bit cue far beyond its training horizon, while the MRV variants show a substantial advantage for the proposed cross-attention direction on this task.
The paper reports multiple training runs, evaluation seeds, environment-specific hyperparameters, computational measurements, and extensive supplementary results.
weaknesses: Theorem 1 is incorrect. The alignment assumption only states that some value row is aligned with each old memory row, whereas the pigeonhole argument identifies some potentially different row having attention weight at least 1/m. The proof then unjustifiably treats these rows as identical and ignores possibly negative contributions from other values. It also assumes the MRV output is unit-normalized without stating or enforcing this, and analyzes a linear attention output although the described MRV includes an FFN/activation. Consequently, the claimed preservation bound does not follow.

Even if the proof were repaired, its stated norm lower bound is non-positive for m>=2; all reported configurations use 5–30 memory tokens. It therefore guarantees no meaningful preservation in the actual experiments, and preservation of vector norm would not itself establish preservation of information.

The architectural novelty is modest: RATE primarily combines RMT-style recurrent memory tokens, Transformer-XL caching, and a simple cross-attention update. Comparisons to closely related recent memory mechanisms such as FFM and SHM are missing, particularly on POPGym, where only DT and basic behavior-cloning baselines are evaluated.

The experiments do not cleanly attribute gains to the three claimed complementary mechanisms. The principal component tests corrupt memory at inference rather than retraining removal variants, and the MRV ablation is confined to T-Maze. Moreover, the reported configurations disable caching on T-Maze and apparently disable MRV on Memory Maze, weakening the claim of a unified three-component architecture.

Several reporting inconsistencies undermine confidence and reproducibility: POPGym is variously described as containing 46 and 48 tasks; Table 2 reports sums of task returns while calling them averages; and the ViZDoom appendix describes 90-step data with a cue disappearing at step 45, whereas a main experiment uses 150 training steps and disappearance at step 90 without explaining the corresponding dataset.

The broad benchmark claims are overstated. MuJoCo uses a custom segment-wise reset of return-to-go and compares against results imported from other papers, so the comparison is not clearly protocol-matched; RATE's average is also below the strongest reported method. Atari covers only four games. These results do not establish a general-purpose state-of-the-art offline-RL method.

Statistical and protocol details remain insufficient for several central conclusions: aggregate POPGym uncertainty is absent, some Memory Maze differences overlap substantially under the reported SEMs, baseline hyperparameters and per-task POPGym configurations are not given, and no significance tests are reported. The inference-time return-to-go update is also unspecified; this is especially important in ViZDoom because reward-derived return tokens could reveal the supposedly hidden color despite rewards being excluded from observations.

strengths: Addresses an important problem: efficient long-horizon memory for offline RL under partial observability.
Evaluates across a broad collection of memory tasks and standard benchmarks, with diverse transformer, recurrent, state-space, behavior-cloning, and offline-RL baselines.
The T-Maze extrapolation results are promising, and the no-MRV comparison provides concrete evidence that the proposed update can help retain a sparse cue.
Provides extensive appendices, multiple-run uncertainty estimates for many experiments, hyperparameters, and useful parameter, latency, and memory measurements.
weaknesses: Theorem 1 is invalid. The proof conflates the attention index having weight at least 1/m with the potentially different index guaranteed to be alpha-aligned, discards possibly negative contributions from other values, and assumes the output memory is normalized although this is not an assumption. Moreover, its stated norm lower bound is usually nonpositive for the reported multi-token memories, so it would be vacuous even if derived correctly. This invalidates a prominently claimed theoretical guarantee.

The MRV's novelty and interpretation are weakly supported. It is essentially standard cross-attention with old memory as queries and updated memory as keys/values; because old memory is not on the value or residual path, the module does not intrinsically preserve information that has already disappeared from the updated values.

The component evidence is incomplete. Inference-time noise corruption shows that a trained model uses its state, not that each component improves learning. Train-from-scratch removals of memory tokens and hidden-state caching are missing across the main environments, while the no-MRV ablation is confined to synthetic T-Maze.

Several comparisons are not controlled. Most notably, RATE resets MuJoCo return-to-go to its maximum at every segment and compares against published baselines using the standard protocol. Baseline tuning budgets and full configurations are not reported, and RATE can disable its feed-forward blocks while transformer baselines retain them. The four-game Atari evaluation is also too narrow for the broad general-purpose claim.

Claims exceed the statistical evidence. RATE's POPGym aggregate advantage over BC-LSTM is only 9.5 versus 9.0 summed across 48 tasks, without aggregate uncertainty; this is mislabeled an average, and RATE loses on many individual tasks. The Memory Maze advantage over RMT is comparable to the reported SEMs, while Minigrid results are aggregated into a boxplot that obscures performance at each extrapolation length.

Reproducibility is weakened by internal inconsistencies: POPGym is alternately described as having 46 and 48 tasks; ViZDoom's pillar disappears at step 45 in the appendix but at step 90 in the main text, while the stated 90-step dataset does not explain the 150-step training experiment; Equation 3 includes an FFN absent from Algorithm 2; hidden-state caching is omitted from the algorithm; and recommended cache-length formulas conflict with several values in the hyperparameter table.

The evaluation is unusually broad, spanning synthetic memory probes, visual and spatial POMDPs, POPGym, Atari, and MuJoCo. RATE shows meaningful gains on ViZDoom-Two-Colors and strong extrapolation on T-Maze.
The paper includes useful MRV variants, memory-corruption and segmentation studies, per-environment hyperparameters, multiple training runs, and computational-efficiency measurements.
The approach substantially reduces peak memory relative to full-context DT while retaining similar inference latency, making it practically relevant.
weaknesses: The central preservation theorem is invalid. The index receiving attention weight at least 1/m need not be the value guaranteed by the alignment assumption; other value terms may have negative inner products; and the proof assumes normalized output memories although the architecture does not enforce this. Moreover, the stated lower bound is nonpositive for typical m>2 and the analyzed operation omits the implemented FFN/multi-head details. Thus, the claimed guarantee is unsupported.

Novelty is incremental: RATE combines RMT-style memory tokens, Transformer-XL caching, and a simple cross-attention update. Since MRV takes values only from the newly computed memory and has no residual path from the old memory, its asserted retention interpretation is not established independently of the flawed theorem.

The component evidence is incomplete. Inference-time noise corruption does not replace train-from-scratch factorial ablations of memory tokens, cached states, and MRV under matched budgets, so the claim that all three mechanisms are complementary is not convincingly isolated.

Comparison fairness is unclear. Hyperparameters and tuning budgets for the authors' RMT/TrXL adaptations are not sufficiently reported, modern memory agents discussed in related work are absent, and Atari/MuJoCo comparisons largely use numbers from other papers. MuJoCo additionally gives RATE a nonstandard per-segment return-to-go reset without applying the same choice to DT.

Several conclusions exceed the evidence: RATE's Memory Maze advantage overlaps baseline uncertainty, POPGym aggregate differences lack uncertainty or significance analysis, the Minigrid boxplot hides performance as a function of extrapolation length, and RATE is not the best method on average in MuJoCo. Three to six training runs are insufficient for the strong state-of-the-art and general-purpose claims without stronger statistical analysis.

Important reporting inconsistencies impair reproducibility: ViZDoom's pillar disappears at step 45 in some sections and step 90 in another; the documented dataset has 90-step trajectories although a headline experiment trains on 150 steps; and POPGym is alternately described as having 46 or 48 tasks. Baseline configurations, inference return targets, and the axis over which SEM is computed are also unclear.

Although the empirical idea remains promising, the false central theorem and substantial evaluation/reporting weaknesses prevent the submission from being technically solid enough for the acceptance threshold.

strengths: Addresses an important problem: efficient long-horizon memory in offline RL, using a plausible combination of segment recurrence, memory tokens, hidden-state caching, and cross-attention-based memory updates.

Empirical coverage is unusually broad, spanning several memory-focused benchmarks, multiple observation modalities, standard control tasks, and substantial length extrapolation. The T-Maze and ViZDoom results are particularly promising.
Includes useful diagnostics, MRV variants, segmentation and hyperparameter studies, multiple training runs, per-task POPGym results, and empirical compute/memory measurements.

The manuscript is generally clear and visually polished, with extensive appendices and a code link. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/iclr2026--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-kzy8ocw0/call-2266df0e2659498cbb11644dea27fe4c/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}
weaknesses: The central MRV preservation theorem is incorrect. The alignment assumption guarantees an aligned value at some index, while the pigeonhole argument guarantees large attention weight at potentially another index; the proof equates them. It also ignores potentially negative contributions from other values and assumes normalization of the updated memory without establishing it.

Even apart from the invalid proof, the stated lower bound is negative and therefore vacuous for the paper's usual setting of multiple memory tokens. Preserving vector norm or geometric alignment would also not establish preservation of task-relevant information, and the claimed empirical alignment condition is not measured.

The MuJoCo comparison is not controlled: RATE resets the target return at every segment, then is compared against published numbers obtained under the standard protocol. Atari and MuJoCo comparisons also mix results from different papers and tuning procedures, undermining the claimed superiority.

Coverage of strong memory baselines is inconsistent. POPGym, a major experiment, compares only with DT, behavior cloning, and random policies, omitting RMT, Transformer-XL, FFM, SHM, and state-space alternatives. The architectural novelty over existing memory-augmented transformers is consequently not convincingly isolated.

The component evidence is incomplete. Inference-time noise is not equivalent to retraining without a component; the main T-Maze configuration disables hidden-state caching, while Memory Maze reports zero MRV heads. A consistent factorial ablation across substantive tasks is needed to support the claimed unified architecture and attribute gains to MRV.

Method and reporting details contain consequential inconsistencies: 46 versus 48 POPGym tasks; quantities called normalized average returns that appear to be sums of raw task scores; cached-state recurrence absent from the formal algorithm; and an FFN present in the MRV equation but absent from its pseudocode. Baseline hyperparameters and model-selection budgets are also insufficiently documented.

Several conclusions exceed the evidence. Memory Maze differences overlap the reported uncertainty, no significance tests are given, RATE is not best on average in MuJoCo, and only four Atari games are evaluated. Thus claims of significant improvement, state-of-the-art performance, and a general-purpose offline-RL architecture are not established.

The efficiency motivation lacks an asymptotic analysis. Because cached hidden-state length can scale with trajectory length, attending to the cache may recover quadratic cumulative cost; comparisons against efficient recurrent and state-space baselines are needed.

strengths: The paper targets an important problem: efficient long-horizon decision-making in partially observable offline RL. Segment-wise processing with recurrent memory is intuitive and computationally attractive.

The evaluation spans several memory-oriented environments and standard offline-RL benchmarks. RATE shows promising results on ViZDoom-Two-Colors and retains a one-bit cue over very long T-Maze sequences.
The authors compare several architectural families, evaluate multiple MRV variants, and report model sizes, latency, GPU memory, run counts, and numerous hyperparameters.
The clean no-MRV comparison on T-Maze provides some evidence that the proposed cross-attention update can improve empirical retention.
weaknesses: The central preservation theorem is invalid. The proof chooses an index receiving attention mass at least 1/m and then incorrectly assumes that this same index is the value guaranteed to be aligned; it also ignores potentially negative contributions from other values and invokes output normalization not implemented in the algorithm. Moreover, for every employed memory size m>=5, the claimed preservation factor 1-sqrt(2(1-alpha/m)) is negative and therefore vacuous.

The architectural novelty is limited: RATE largely combines RMT-style memory tokens, Transformer-XL caching, and an additional cross-attention block. The MRV has neither an explicit gate nor a residual path carrying old memory, so its interpretation as a retention valve is not technically established.

The method is underspecified and internally inconsistent. Cached-state integration is absent from the algorithms and equations; Equation 3 includes an FFN omitted by Algorithm 2; the recommended cache-length formula conflicts with several configurations in Table 8; and Memory Maze uses zero MRV heads despite broad claims about the complete architecture.

The component evidence is incomplete. Most memory-token and cache analyses corrupt a trained model at inference, an out-of-distribution intervention that cannot replace retraining without each component. A factorial, capacity-matched ablation of memory tokens, caching, and MRV is missing across the substantive environments.

The headline 9,600-step T-Maze result overstates the evidence. This modified task requires copying one bit through repeated filler observations, supplies an explicit junction flag, and uses only successful oracle demonstrations. The appendix also shows several recurrent or memory baselines reaching essentially perfect extrapolation when trained at selected shorter horizons, so the main comparison partly reflects optimization failure at the chosen long training horizon rather than uniquely superior memory.

The POPGym analysis is unreliable: the manuscript alternates between 46 and 48 tasks, calls a sum of task returns an average normalized score, and reports only a tiny aggregate advantage over BC-LSTM without uncertainty or significance analysis. Strong memory-specific baselines such as FFM and SHM—and even RMT/Transformer-XL used elsewhere in the paper—are omitted.

The standard-benchmark claims are overstated and not based on controlled comparisons. MuJoCo uses a RATE-specific return-to-go resetting procedure while most baselines are imported from other papers; RATE's reported mean trails several methods and appears best on only 2 of 9 tasks. The Atari evaluation covers only four games and similarly mixes externally reported results.

Statistical and reproducibility support is insufficient for the breadth of the claims. Most memory experiments use only 3–6 training runs, the level over which SEM is computed is unclear, no significance tests are given, Atari/MuJoCo run counts are omitted, and detailed baseline configurations and tuning budgets are not reported.

Several auxiliary arguments are not valid evidence: attention maps do not demonstrate causal information retention, and OracleDT with privileged input is a reference model rather than a mathematical or empirical upper bound. Additional factual inconsistencies, such as claiming up to a 7.7% parameter reduction when Table 12 shows at most 2.91%, further reduce confidence.

strengths: Addresses the important problem of long-horizon memory in partially observable offline RL with an intuitive segment-recurrent architecture. The complete manuscript and appendix were inspected :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/iclr2026--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-k7anyg3c/call-50a0ae0105874971af70bd8593f1bec2/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}.

The evaluation is unusually broad, covering synthetic memory diagnostics, visual navigation, POPGym, Atari, and MuJoCo, with transformer, recurrent, state-space, behavior-cloning, and offline-RL comparisons.

The T-Maze and ViZDoom results provide promising evidence that recurrent memory can extrapolate substantially beyond the training context; the reported 9,600-step evaluation is particularly interesting.

The paper includes MRV variants, memory-corruption experiments, architectural sweeps, multiple training runs, hyperparameter tables, and computational measurements. RATE also reduces memory consumption relative to a full-context DT in several experiments.
The exposition is generally understandable, code is linked, and no material ethical concerns arise from the benchmark-based study.
weaknesses: The central MRV preservation theorem is invalid. The proof selects an attention index with weight at least 1/m and then incorrectly assumes that this same index is the one guaranteed to be aligned. It also discards potentially negative contributions from all other values and assumes normalization of the MRV output without establishing or implementing it. Moreover, for every used setting with m>=2, the claimed preservation factor 1-sqrt(2(1-alpha/m)) is non-positive and therefore vacuous. A norm lower bound would not itself establish preservation of memory content. Consequently, the conclusion's claimed theoretical guarantee is unsupported.

The architectural novelty is limited: memory tokens and hidden-state caching come directly from RMT and Transformer-XL, while MRV is a relatively simple cross-attention update. Since old memory only supplies queries and is not directly retained through a residual or gate, the claimed preservation mechanism is especially unclear. Comparisons with closely related learned-memory methods such as FFM, SHM, and GTrXL are absent.

The component evidence is incomplete. Corrupting activations with random noise at inference creates an out-of-distribution intervention and is not a substitute for retraining clean architectural ablations. MRV configurations are evaluated principally on the simple T-Maze task, and the complete three-component design is not consistently used: T-Maze disables cached states, while Memory Maze reports zero MRV heads.

Several empirical claims are overstated. Memory Maze improvements over RMT and TrXL are small relative to reported uncertainty; Minigrid results are aggregated over grid sizes and obscure scale-specific behavior; and the appendix shows some recurrent baselines generalizing strongly from selected short training lengths. These results do not establish consistent superiority across memory tasks.

The POPGym evaluation has important reporting and comparison problems. The manuscript alternates between 46 and 48 tasks, while the table contains 48 and the 33/15 split also totals 48. Values described as average normalized scores exceed the task score range and appear to be sums. RATE's aggregate advantage over BC-LSTM is small, yet no uncertainty or significance is reported for the aggregate, and strong memory baselines such as RMT, TrXL, FFM, SHM, or state-space models are omitted.

The general-purpose offline-RL claims are weakly supported. Atari covers only four games. MuJoCo comparisons mostly reuse numbers from other papers while RATE employs a modified per-segment return-conditioning procedure; run counts and evaluation seeds for Atari and MuJoCo are omitted. RATE's MuJoCo average is also below the strongest reported Decision Mamba result. Most memory datasets are successful or high-quality demonstrations, so robustness to mixed-quality data, limited coverage, or other core offline-RL difficulties is not tested.

Reproducibility remains incomplete despite the linked code. The algorithms do not formally specify hidden-state caching, gradient detachment across segments, positional handling, or memory initialization/reset behavior; baseline architectures and tuning budgets are largely absent. Cache-length recommendations also conflict with reported configurations. Given the invalid theory and these unresolved evaluation issues, the work is not competitive at the stated acceptance threshold.

strengths: The manuscript :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/iclr2026--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-34zvs0m4/call-884e708a281a4251af74cf444e9af0d4/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"} addresses an important problem: efficient long-horizon memory for offline RL under partial observability.

RATE is an intuitive combination of recurrent memory tokens, cached hidden states, and a cross-attention memory update. Its segment-wise processing also offers meaningful memory-efficiency advantages over a full-context Decision Transformer.

The empirical scope is unusually broad. It includes several memory-intensive environments, direct transformer-memory baselines, recurrent and state-space baselines, standard control benchmarks, multiple seeds, and long-horizon extrapolation tests.

The strongest evidence is on T-Maze and ViZDoom. RATE retains useful performance far beyond its training context, and the trained MRV variants substantially outperform the no-MRV model on long T-Maze corridors. Hyperparameter, corruption, architecture, and efficiency studies add useful diagnostic evidence.
No significant ethical concerns are apparent for the benchmark-based contribution.
weaknesses: Theorem 1 and its claimed preservation guarantee are invalid. The alignment assumption provides some aligned value index, while the pigeonhole argument provides a potentially different high-attention index; the proof incorrectly identifies them. It also ignores potentially negative contributions from the other values and assumes the attention output is unit-normalized without establishing this. Moreover, with the actual memory sizes m=5–30, the stated lower-bound factor is nonpositive, so it does not guarantee preservation of any positive fraction. The claimed empirical validity of the alignment assumption is not measured.

The method is not specified consistently enough to reproduce from the paper. Hidden-state caching is absent from the main algorithm and equations, with insufficient detail about its layer-wise use and gradient handling. Equation 3 includes an FFN, whereas Algorithm 2 and the theorem omit it; the reported MRV activation is also absent from both. The initialization is described both as learned memory embeddings and as a Gaussian sample.

Novelty is moderate: memory tokens largely follow RMT, caching follows Transformer-XL, and MRV is a relatively direct cross-attention update. The paper needs stronger comparisons with closely related modern memory mechanisms and training-time removals of each component across multiple tasks. Inference-time noise corruption introduces distribution shift and is not a clean substitute for such ablations.

Baseline fairness and reproducibility remain unclear. Only RATE hyperparameters are reported despite a claim that baseline settings appear in the appendix; parameter counts are supplied only against DT, and tuning budgets or selection protocols are not documented. Several standard-benchmark comparisons reuse numbers from other papers rather than controlled runs.

The general-purpose claims are overstated. Atari covers only four games. MuJoCo uses a nonstandard return-to-go reset at every segment while comparing against literature results obtained with standard protocols; RATE's average is below several listed methods, and run/seed counts for Atari and MuJoCo are omitted.

Some summaries obscure mixed results. POPGym is inconsistently described as containing 46 versus 48 tasks, and Table 2 labels sums of task returns as averages; the aggregate gain over BC-LSTM is small and RATE loses on numerous individual tasks. Minigrid reports only a boxplot aggregated over grid sizes, which does not substantiate consistent extrapolation at every scale. Claims of statistically significant or consistent superiority are made without corresponding hypothesis tests.

OracleDT is not a genuine upper bound: supplying one privileged bit to a different architecture produces a useful diagnostic reference, but it cannot mathematically upper-bound RATE's achievable performance. Overall, the promising empirical results prevent a strong reject, but the false central theoretical claim and unresolved evaluation issues make the submission insufficiently sound for acceptance.

strengths: The paper addresses an important problem: efficient long-horizon memory for offline reinforcement learning under partial observability.
RATE is intuitive and practically motivated, combining recurrent memory tokens, cached hidden states, and a cross-attention retention module.

The experimental scope is unusually broad, covering several memory benchmarks, very long T-Maze extrapolation, Atari, and MuJoCo, with comparisons to transformer, recurrent, state-space, and conventional offline-RL baselines.

The strongest results—particularly T-Maze extrapolation and ViZDoom-Two-Colors—suggest that the architecture can preserve task-relevant information beyond a fixed transformer context. The MRV-variant comparison also provides useful empirical evidence.
The appendices provide substantial implementation information, including hyperparameters, environment construction, run counts, parameter counts, and computational measurements.
weaknesses: The central MRV preservation theorem is incorrect. The proof selects an attention index with weight at least 1/m and then assumes it is the index guaranteed by the existential alpha-alignment condition; these indices need not coincide. It also discards potentially negative contributions from other values and assumes the MRV output is unit-normalized although only the incoming memory is assumed normalized. Moreover, for the memory sizes used experimentally, the stated lower bound is generally negative and therefore vacuous. Thus the claimed theoretical guarantee is unsupported.

Architectural novelty is limited: RATE largely combines RMT-style prefix/suffix memory tokens, Transformer-XL caching, and standard cross-attention. The experiments do not isolate whether the proposed MRV adds value over a carefully matched combination of the first two mechanisms.

The main component study corrupts trained memories with noise at inference, introducing distribution shift rather than comparing components removed and retrained end-to-end. MRV is primarily validated on the synthetic one-bit T-Maze, with no convincing ablation across the more realistic memory environments.

Several empirical claims are overstated. Memory Maze differences overlap the reported uncertainty; no significance tests are provided; RATE is below the strongest MuJoCo method on average; and Table 3 appears to show RATE as best on 2/9 MuJoCo tasks rather than the claimed 3/9.

The POPGym reporting is internally inconsistent: the manuscript alternates between 46 and 48 tasks, while the 33/15 split totals 48. Table 2 calls values such as 9.5 average normalized returns even though they appear to be sums of per-task returns. RATE also loses to BC-LSTM on many individual tasks, and strong POPGym memory baselines or the PPO-GRU data-generating policy are not reported.

Comparison fairness is insufficiently controlled. RATE receives task-specific architectural choices such as removing the transformer FFN, while matched baselines do not; the MuJoCo evaluation resets return-to-go at every segment without applying the same strategy to DT; and several standard-benchmark results are imported from other papers without demonstrating identical evaluation conditions.

The headline extrapolation evidence relies heavily on a highly structured T-Maze that reduces to delayed one-bit recall, supplies an explicit junction flag, and uses only successful oracle trajectories. Minigrid performance is aggregated over grid sizes in a box plot, preventing verification of the claimed consistent performance through 501-by-501 grids.

Important implementation details remain ambiguous or absent from the formal method, including how cached hidden states enter the transformer, whether initial memory is learned or randomly sampled, masking and positional encoding across segments, gradient truncation, and per-task POPGym configurations. These issues impede independent reproduction.

strengths: RATE addresses an important problem in offline RL: retaining information across horizons that exceed a transformer's context window. Its segment-wise recurrence, memory tokens, cached states, and retention module form a coherent architecture.

The evaluation is unusually broad, covering several memory-focused environments, POPGym, Atari, and MuJoCo. The T-Maze extrapolation to 9,600 steps and ViZDoom results provide meaningful evidence of long-range recall.
The paper includes useful diagnostics and ablations involving MRV variants, memory corruption, segment configurations, transformer hyperparameters, an oracle, and an associative-retrieval task.
Environment details, RATE hyperparameters, run counts for the memory experiments, and computational measurements are reported, supporting partial reproducibility.
weaknesses: The central MRV preservation theorem is invalid. The proof conflates the index guaranteed to receive attention mass of at least 1/m with the potentially different index guaranteed to be alpha-aligned. It also ignores negative contributions from other value vectors. Moreover, output-row normalization is assumed but not implemented or established, and the claimed lower bound is non-positive for m >= 2, making the stated preservation interpretation vacuous even if the derivation were repaired.

The architectural novelty is modest: RATE primarily combines RMT-style memory tokens, Transformer-XL caching, and conventional cross-attention. Direct comparisons with highly relevant memory mechanisms such as FFM and SHM are missing, despite their discussion in related work.

The ablations do not establish that the three proposed mechanisms are complementary. Most memory-token and cache ablations inject noise only at inference, introducing distribution shift instead of retraining clean component removals. Some reported configurations disable cached states or MRV entirely, further weakening the unified-architecture claim.

Comparison fairness is insufficiently controlled. RATE receives extensive task-specific tuning, while corresponding baseline hyperparameters and selection procedures are not reported. MuJoCo uses a nonstandard return-to-go reset for RATE while comparator numbers are imported from prior papers, and Atari/MuJoCo run and seed counts are omitted.

Several claims exceed the evidence. RATE's average MuJoCo score is below multiple reported methods, Memory Maze improvements overlap uncertainty intervals, and no significance tests support many claimed gains. The POPGym 'average' aggregates are actually sums of subset scores, and the paper inconsistently reports 46 versus 48 POPGym tasks.

Important reproducibility details remain unclear, including gradient flow or detachment through recurrent memory, memory normalization required by the theory, positional handling during extreme extrapolation, baseline architectures, and the hierarchy used to compute standard errors. Efficiency comparisons are also confounded by disabling RATE's feed-forward blocks while retaining them in transformer baselines.

strengths: RATE addresses an important problem and offers an intuitive hybrid of recurrent memory tokens, cached hidden states, and a cross-attention Memory Retention Valve.
The empirical scope is broad, covering several memory-intensive environments and standard offline-RL benchmarks. The long-horizon T-Maze and ViZDoom results are particularly promising.
The manuscript provides numerous ablations, multi-run uncertainty estimates, hyperparameters, parameter counts, and computational-efficiency measurements.
weaknesses: Theorem 1 is invalid as written. The proof conflates the value token guaranteed to be aligned with the token receiving attention weight at least 1/m, ignores potentially negative contributions from other value tokens, and assumes normalization of the output memory without establishing or enforcing it. Its norm lower bound is also generally non-positive for m>=2 and therefore vacuous. Consequently, the claimed memory-preservation guarantee is unsupported.

The component evidence is incomplete. Memory-token and hidden-cache contributions are assessed by injecting noise only at inference, which creates distribution shift rather than providing controlled, retrained ablations. Only the MRV removal is a convincing component ablation.

Several reporting and protocol problems weaken the empirical claims. The POPGym quantities described as averages are sums over tasks; RATE's 9.5 versus BC-LSTM's 9.0 corresponds to only about 0.012 mean improvement per task, without aggregate uncertainty or significance testing. The manuscript also inconsistently refers to 46 and 48 POPGym tasks.

The standard-benchmark comparisons are not fully controlled. Many baseline results are imported from prior papers, while RATE uses a custom per-segment return-to-go reset on MuJoCo that is not evaluated for the baselines. RATE is competitive but not best on average, so the general-purpose superiority claim is overstated.

The implementation description is internally incomplete: hidden-state caching is absent from the main algorithm and equations, the MRV algorithm does not match the FFN-based equation, and baseline hyperparameters are not reported comparably. Closely related modern memory architectures cited in the paper are also omitted from experiments.

strengths: RATE addresses an important offline-RL problem with a clear architecture combining segment recurrence, memory tokens, hidden-state caching, and a Memory Retention Valve.

The empirical scope is unusually broad, covering multiple synthetic and visual memory tasks, all reported POPGym variants, Atari, and MuJoCo. The T-Maze results extending to 9,600 steps provide especially compelling evidence of long-horizon extrapolation.

RATE is consistently strong on the central memory benchmarks, including ViZDoom-Two-Colors, Memory Maze, Minigrid-Memory, and aggregate POPGym performance, while remaining competitive on reactive and fully observable tasks.

The paper includes useful MRV comparisons, memory-corruption studies, segmentation and architecture ablations, multiple-run uncertainty estimates, detailed hyperparameters, and parameter, latency, and memory-footprint measurements.
The presentation is generally clear and the computational advantages over a long-context Decision Transformer strengthen the practical case for the approach.
weaknesses: Theorem 1 is not valid under its stated assumptions. The value vector guaranteed to be aligned need not be the index receiving attention weight at least 1/m; contributions from other values can also be negatively aligned. The proof additionally assumes the MRV output rows are normalized without establishing this. Consequently, the claimed preservation guarantee does not follow, and its norm lower bound is generally vacuous for multiple memory tokens.

The architectural novelty is moderate: memory tokens and hidden-state caching come directly from RMT and Transformer-XL, while MRV is a relatively standard cross-attention update. A full trained factorial ablation separating tokens, caching, and MRV is missing; inference-time noise introduces distribution shift and is not an adequate substitute.

Baseline coverage is uneven. POPGym omits strong memory-oriented alternatives such as RMT, Transformer-XL, FFM, SHM, and state-space models, while Atari and MuJoCo comparisons largely reuse results from other papers rather than providing controlled, equally tuned reruns.

Some claims are overstated. RATE is not state of the art on average in MuJoCo, and the evidence does not yet establish it as a general-purpose offline-RL architecture. The manuscript also inconsistently refers to 46 versus 48 POPGym tasks and labels what appears to be a sum of task scores as an average.

Reproducibility details remain incomplete for a central component: hidden-state caching is absent from the main algorithm and equations, and cache detachment, reset behavior, positional handling, and baseline-specific hyperparameters are insufficiently specified. Several results use only three training runs, with no significance testing.

strengths: The paper targets an important problem: retaining long-range information in offline partially observable RL while avoiding full-trajectory self-attention. RATE is conceptually coherent and easy to understand as recurrent memory tokens, cached hidden states, and a selective memory-update module.

The strongest experiments are compelling. RATE preserves a one-bit cue over T-Maze horizons far beyond its training context and substantially improves return and color-conditioned balance in ViZDoom-Two-Colors.

The empirical scope is unusually broad, spanning five memory-oriented suites, Atari, and MuJoCo, with transformer, recurrent, value-based, and state-space baselines. The paper also reports multiple runs, architectural ablations, resource usage, and extensive implementation details.

The presentation and figures are generally clear, and the efficiency measurements demonstrate meaningful GPU-memory savings relative to full-context DT. Source reviewed: :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/iclr2026--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-4mrgwsxy/call-3b33f1e23e974cf6825c71ccb033d217/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}
weaknesses: Theorem 1 is invalid as written. The value index guaranteed to be alpha-aligned need not be the index receiving attention mass at least 1/m; the remaining values can contribute negative inner products; and the proof assumes the MRV output is normalized although no such assumption or operation is given. Moreover, for m>=2 the stated norm lower bound is generally nonpositive and therefore vacuous. Consequently, the claimed memory-preservation guarantee does not follow.

The architectural novelty is modest: most of RATE consists of combining RMT-style memory tokens and Transformer-XL caching, while MRV is standard cross-attention from old to updated memory. Particularly relevant modern memory agents such as FFM and SHM are discussed but not compared experimentally.

Several claims overstate the results. POPGym's reported 9.5 versus 9.0 appears to be a sum over tasks rather than the claimed average, amounts to roughly 0.01 per task, and has no aggregate uncertainty analysis; the manuscript also inconsistently reports 46 versus 48 tasks. Memory Maze gains over RMT are small with overlapping uncertainty, and Minigrid results are aggregated across grid sizes rather than reported by extrapolation distance.

The evidence for general-purpose superiority is weak. RATE's average MuJoCo score trails several reported methods, Atari covers only four games, and MuJoCo uses a nonstandard segmentwise return-to-go reset that complicates comparison with externally sourced baseline results.

The component evidence is incomplete. Inference-time noise injection creates distribution shift and is not a substitute for retraining models without each component; MRV variants are principally tested on the simple T-Maze; and OracleDT is a privileged-information baseline, not a valid upper bound.

Important reproducibility ambiguities remain: hidden-state caching is omitted from the main algorithm, the MRV equation includes an FFN absent from its pseudocode, initial memory is described both as learned and randomly sampled, baseline configurations are not documented comparably, and stated cache-length recommendations conflict with several values in the hyperparameter table.

strengths: The paper addresses an important offline-RL problem with an intuitive architecture combining recurrent memory tokens, cached hidden states, and segment-wise processing. The presentation is generally readable and well illustrated. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/iclr2026--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-yw01zyhf/call-470d605de6604838a8bcf400c1e3db64/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}

The empirical scope is unusually broad, covering several dedicated memory environments, image and vector observations, discrete and continuous control, long-horizon extrapolation, and standard Atari/MuJoCo benchmarks.

There is meaningful empirical evidence for the proposed mechanism: for example, MRV-CA-2 achieves 0.90±0.07 success at T-Maze length 900 versus 0.61±0.07 without MRV, and RATE exhibits promising extrapolation far beyond its training horizon.

The appendices provide dataset descriptions, encoders, RATE hyperparameters, run counts, hardware, parameter counts, and computational measurements. No significant ethical concerns are apparent for these benchmark-only experiments.
weaknesses: Theorem 1, a stated central contribution, is invalid. The aligned value row guaranteed by the α-alignment assumption need not be the high-attention row selected by the pigeonhole argument; other weighted inner products may be negative and cannot simply be discarded; and the proof assumes the MRV output is unit-normalized although the method never establishes this. Moreover, with the actual number of memory tokens m≥5, the claimed preservation lower bound is negative and therefore vacuous. The assertion that α-alignment holds empirically is unsupported by measurements.

The core method is incompletely and inconsistently specified. Hidden-state caching is absent from Algorithms 1–2 and the mathematical definition; Equation 3 includes an FFN that Algorithm 2 omits; required normalization is not implemented; and it is unclear whether initial memory is sampled or learned, where gradients are detached across segments, and how caching and positional information operate at inference. These omissions impede reproduction and interpretation.

The novelty is relatively incremental: memory tokens largely follow RMT, caching follows Transformer-XL, and MRV is a simple cross-attention update without an explicit residual path from old memory. The paper does not convincingly establish why this combination is fundamentally distinct from prior recurrent-memory transformers.

Several comparisons are confounded. Atari and MuJoCo baselines are imported from other papers rather than evaluated in one controlled implementation; RATE uses a segment-wise return-to-go reset on MuJoCo that is not applied to DT; RATE alone is allowed to remove the transformer FFN; and baseline tuning budgets and configurations are not reported. Closely related memory approaches such as FFM and SHM are discussed but omitted from POPGym comparisons.

The conclusions overstate the numerical evidence. RATE's MuJoCo average of 78.5 is below Decision Mamba (83.2), MambaDM (79.0), and TT (78.9), and RATE is top-1 on only 2/9 tasks despite the text claiming 3/9. Memory Maze differences overlap substantially, while Minigrid shows TrXL as competitive. No paired significance tests support the broad state-of-the-art or general-purpose claims.

POPGym reporting contains material inconsistencies: the manuscript alternates between 46 and 48 tasks while the stated 33+15 split and Table 9 contain 48. Table 2's reported 9.54 is the sum of 48 task returns, not an average as claimed; the actual RATE mean is about 0.199, and its overall mean advantage over BC-LSTM is only about 0.009. ViZDoom descriptions likewise disagree about cue-disappearance times and training-trajectory lengths.

The component ablation mainly corrupts a trained model with out-of-distribution noise, which does not isolate what each mechanism contributes when trained fairly. Retrained factorial ablations of memory tokens, caching, and MRV are needed. OracleDT is also a privileged-information reference, not a valid upper bound.

The most dramatic extrapolation result comes from a synthetic T-Maze requiring storage of one bit and providing an explicit junction flag. It demonstrates persistent recall but does not by itself substantiate claims of high-capacity long-horizon memory; gains on the more complex tasks are generally smaller.

The empirical scope is broad, spanning synthetic memory diagnostics, image- and vector-based POMDPs, POPGym, Atari, and MuJoCo, with transformer, recurrent, value-based, and state-space baselines.
The T-Maze extrapolation and ViZDoom cue-retention experiments provide compelling evidence that RATE can preserve simple sparse information far beyond a standard transformer's context window.
The appendix includes multiple training runs, MRV variants, memory-corruption tests, architectural ablations, parameter counts, and computational-efficiency measurements.
weaknesses: Theorem 1 is false as written. The proof selects an attention index with weight at least 1/m and incorrectly assumes that it is also the existentially aligned value index; it ignores potentially negative contributions from all other values and assumes normalization of the MRV output although only the incoming memory is normalized. Moreover, for the employed m>=2, the claimed preserved-fraction coefficient is non-positive and hence vacuous. The paper's theoretical preservation claim is therefore unsupported.

The architectural novelty is modest: RATE primarily combines RMT-style memory tokens, Transformer-XL caching, and standard cross-attention. The formulation is also incomplete and inconsistent: caching is absent from the algorithms, Equation 3 includes an FFN omitted by Algorithm 2, and the supposedly learned initial memory is shown as a Gaussian sample.

The claim that RATE jointly uses three complementary mechanisms is misleading. Table 8 disables cached states on T-Maze and apparently disables MRV on Memory Maze, so reported results come from task-specific subsets rather than one unified architecture.

The central ablations are insufficiently causal. Inference-time noise creates distribution shift and does not replace retraining genuine component-removal variants; MRV is principally isolated on the simple one-bit T-Maze task, with no matched ablation across the broader benchmarks.

Several performance claims exceed the evidence. Memory Maze differences have overlapping uncertainty, Minigrid does not clearly dominate TrXL, and no significance tests support repeated uses of 'significantly.' Table 3 places RATE below several methods on average and appears to show only two, not the claimed three, best-of-nine MuJoCo scores.

POPGym reporting is problematic: the paper alternates between 46 and 48 tasks, while the 33/15 split totals 48. The values labeled as average returns in Table 2 are actually sums of the 48 Table 9 scores. RATE's true mean is approximately 0.199 versus 0.187 for BC-LSTM, a small advantage reported without aggregate uncertainty and inconsistent with claims of a consistent failure by competing models.

Baseline fairness is unclear. RATE receives environment-specific tuning and optional FFN removal, whereas baseline configurations and tuning budgets are not documented comparably. Atari and MuJoCo comparisons import results from other papers, and RATE additionally uses a nonstandard per-segment return-reset scheme on MuJoCo that is not applied to DT, confounding architectural conclusions.

Reproducibility remains incomplete despite the extensive appendix: actual random seeds, per-baseline hyperparameters, POPGym dataset sizes and per-task configurations, inference return-conditioning choices, positional treatment, and gradient flow through recurrent memory are not specified.

strengths: Addresses an important problem: scalable long-horizon memory for offline reinforcement learning, with an intuitive combination of recurrent memory tokens, cached states, and a retention module. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/iclr2026--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-npm2svos/call-92f683b1e4ef45c6b5d944000ac03d29/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}

The evaluation is unusually broad, covering several memory-focused environments, POPGym, Atari, and MuJoCo. The T-Maze extrapolation to horizons substantially longer than those used in training is particularly compelling.
Includes relevant transformer, recurrent, and state-space baselines, along with MRV variants, memory-corruption studies, segmentation ablations, and computational measurements.
The architecture and environments are generally explained clearly, and the appendix provides useful hyperparameters, dataset-generation details, run counts, and a code link.
weaknesses: Theorem 1 is invalid. The alignment assumption guarantees an aligned value row exists, while the pigeonhole argument identifies a potentially different high-attention row; the proof incorrectly treats them as the same row and also ignores potentially negative contributions from other values. It additionally assumes normalized output-memory rows without establishing this. For the actual memory-token counts, the stated norm lower bound is generally nonpositive and therefore vacuous. This invalidates the paper's claimed theoretical memory-preservation guarantee.

Component attribution is incomplete. Inference-time noise creates out-of-distribution activations and is not a substitute for retraining clean component-removal ablations. The full factorial contribution of memory tokens, cached states, and MRV is not demonstrated across tasks; indeed, caching is disabled for T-Maze and MRV is disabled for Memory Maze.

Comparison fairness is insufficiently controlled. Baseline architectures and tuning budgets are not reported comparably, while RATE receives extensive task-specific configuration. MuJoCo uses a RATE-specific return-to-go reset at every segment but compares against published baselines using the standard protocol, without applying or ablating this choice on DT.

Several broad claims exceed the evidence: Atari covers only four games, RATE's average MuJoCo score is below the strongest reported baseline, many gains are modest relative to uncertainty, and no significance tests are provided. The manuscript also inconsistently reports 46 versus 48 POPGym tasks.

The architectural novelty is incremental relative to RMT, Transformer-XL, and prior gated recurrent-memory models: the principal new element is a straightforward cross-attention update, whose theoretical justification fails.

Much of the memory evaluation uses oracle-generated successful trajectories or demonstrations from strong recurrent agents, making the setup closer to sequence imitation than challenging offline RL. Robustness to mixed-quality datasets, coverage limitations, and offline distribution shift is not established.

Reproducibility remains incomplete despite the code link: only RATE hyperparameters are tabulated, the search and checkpoint-selection procedures are unclear, POPGym settings are shown for only one representative task, and run/uncertainty protocols for Atari and MuJoCo are not fully specified.

strengths: The manuscript :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/iclr2026--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-oi6q3e1h/call-648aea0537574c0cb6790a9addc1652b/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"} addresses an important problem: scalable memory for offline RL under partial observability. The combination of recurrent memory tokens, cached hidden states, and a selective update module is intuitive and practically relevant.

The empirical coverage is unusually broad, spanning T-Maze, ViZDoom-Two-Colors, Minigrid-Memory, Memory Maze, POPGym, Atari, and MuJoCo, with transformer, recurrent, state-space, behavior-cloning, and offline-RL baselines.
The strongest results are compelling: RATE retains cues far beyond its training horizon in T-Maze, performs well under large Minigrid extrapolation, and achieves strong, balanced ViZDoom performance.

The paper includes useful MRV-variant comparisons, memory-corruption analyses, segmentation and architectural ablations, efficiency measurements, encoder specifications, hyperparameters, run counts, and dataset-collection details.
weaknesses: The central preservation theorem is invalid. The alignment assumption guarantees an aligned value index for each memory row, while the pigeonhole argument identifies a potentially different high-attention index; the proof incorrectly equates them. It also discards possibly negative contributions from all other values and assumes normalization of post-MRV vectors without establishing it. Moreover, for the employed memory sizes m=5–30 and α≤1, the claimed retained fraction 1−sqrt(2(1−α/m)) is negative and therefore vacuous. The analysis also omits the implemented FFN and multi-head operations. Consequently, the claimed theoretical guarantee is unsupported.

Architectural novelty is moderate: memory-token recurrence and hidden-state caching largely inherit RMT and Transformer-XL, leaving the relatively simple cross-attention MRV as the main new element. The broken theoretical analysis makes its distinction less convincing.

Several important comparisons are missing. In particular, directly relevant modern memory agents such as FFM and SHM are discussed but not evaluated, and POPGym comparisons include only DT, BC-MLP, and BC-LSTM rather than RMT, Transformer-XL, state-space models, or other specialized memory methods.

Some conclusions exceed the evidence. The POPGym aggregate advantage over BC-LSTM is only 9.5 versus 9.0 across 48 tasks and has no aggregate uncertainty or significance analysis; the paper also inconsistently reports 46 versus 48 tasks. Memory Maze intervals overlap substantially. RATE's MuJoCo average is below several competitors, and the Atari study covers only four games, so the broad state-of-the-art/general-purpose claims are not established.

The component evidence is incomplete: inference-time replacement with noise creates distribution shift and is not equivalent to retraining without a component. A factorial train-time ablation of memory tokens, cached states, and MRV across multiple environments is needed; the decisive MRV comparison is confined to the simple one-bit T-Maze.

Evaluation and reproducibility details remain ambiguous. The nonstandard MuJoCo procedure resets return-to-go to its maximum at every segment but is neither ablated nor applied to comparison methods; most competing standard-benchmark scores are imported from other papers; baseline tuning budgets and selection rules are unspecified; POPGym hyperparameters are not given per task; and it is unclear whether reported SEM captures variation across training runs or primarily correlated inference episodes. Several dense figures are also difficult to read at normal scale.

strengths: The paper addresses an important limitation of transformer policies in partially observable, long-horizon offline reinforcement learning.

RATE is a conceptually simple hybrid of recurrent memory tokens, cached hidden states, and selective memory updates. The reported T-Maze extrapolation to substantially longer horizons than seen during training is notable.
The empirical study is broad, covering several memory-focused environments as well as Atari and MuJoCo, with transformer, recurrent, state-space, behavior-cloning, and value-based baselines.

The manuscript provides useful component studies, multiple MRV variants, architectural ablations, parameter counts, runtime and memory measurements, environment descriptions, hyperparameters, and a code link.
weaknesses: The central theoretical result is invalid. The alpha-alignment assumption guarantees an aligned value row exists, while the pigeonhole argument guarantees that potentially another row receives attention at least 1/m; the proof incorrectly treats these indices as identical. It also discards potentially negative contributions from all other value rows and assumes the MRV output is normalized although only the incoming memory is assumed normalized. Moreover, with the reported memory sizes, the resulting norm lower bound is negative and therefore vacuous. Embedding norm or proximity would not itself establish preservation of task-relevant information even if the derivation were repaired. Thus the claimed memory-preservation guarantee in the contributions and conclusion is unsupported.

The architectural novelty is incremental relative to RMT and Transformer-XL: the main new component is a straightforward cross-attention update between old and proposed memory tokens. Its exact specification is also inconsistent or incomplete: Equation 3 includes an FFN that Algorithm 2 omits, and the integration and recurrence of cached hidden states are not fully specified.

Several empirical claims are overstated. POPGym Table 2 labels sums across tasks as average normalized returns: the reported RATE value 9.5 is the sum of the 48 Table 9 scores, whose actual mean is about 0.20. RATE's aggregate advantage over BC-LSTM is only about 0.012 per task, yet no paired uncertainty or statistical test is reported. Similarly, overlapping uncertainty in Memory Maze and RATE's fifth-ranked MuJoCo average do not support broad state-of-the-art or consistent-superiority language.

Baseline fairness and reproducibility are insufficiently documented. Only RATE hyperparameters are tabulated; baseline configurations, tuning budgets, actual seeds, and detailed data-generation settings are missing. Some standard-benchmark comparisons use numbers from other papers, and MuJoCo uses a method-specific return-to-go reset, weakening controlled comparisons. Modern long-memory methods mentioned in related work are not evaluated or explicitly justified as inapplicable.

The component evidence is incomplete. Inference-time replacement with noise creates distribution shift and does not isolate what would happen if a component were removed during training. The decisive MRV ablation is confined to the synthetic T-Maze, with no trained no-MRV comparison on the richer memory environments. The privileged-information OracleDT is also not a genuine upper bound on achievable policy performance.

The evaluation relies heavily on successful or strong-policy trajectories and does not study robustness to dataset quality, coverage, or suboptimal behavior, limiting the conclusions about offline RL rather than long-context behavior cloning. Minigrid results are aggregated into a boxplot across grid sizes, which cannot establish the claimed consistently high performance over the entire extrapolation range.

strengths: Addresses an important problem: efficient long-horizon memory for offline reinforcement learning under partial observability.

RATE is a practical combination of segment recurrence, memory tokens, cached hidden states, and cross-attention. It shows strong results on ViZDoom and useful extrapolation on T-Maze while reducing GPU memory relative to full-context DT.

The evaluation spans several memory environments, standard control benchmarks, and multiple model families. The appendix provides environment descriptions, hyperparameters, ablations, and efficiency measurements.
The MRV configuration comparison provides some empirical evidence that the proposed cross-attention update helps on long T-Maze corridors.
weaknesses: The central MRV theorem and proof are invalid. The maximum-attention index need not be the value satisfying the alignment condition; other attention terms may contribute negative inner products; normalization of the updated memory is not established; and the analyzed map omits the stated FFN/activation. Furthermore, for the multi-token settings used, the claimed retained-fraction lower bound is non-positive and therefore vacuous. A Frobenius-norm bound would not establish preservation of information in any case.

The main architectural novelty is limited: MRV is essentially standard cross-attention with old memory as queries and new memory as keys/values, without a direct residual or gating path that guarantees retention. The remaining components closely follow RMT and Transformer-XL.

The component ablations are insufficient. Most replace memory or cached states with noise only at inference, introducing distribution shift rather than comparing models trained without each component. The clean MRV ablation is largely confined to synthetic T-Maze, and the reported Memory Maze configuration uses zero MRV heads.

The broad empirical claims are overstated. POPGym lacks RMT, Transformer-XL, FFM, SHM, and other relevant memory baselines; Atari covers only four games; and RATE is not best on average in MuJoCo. Moreover, RATE resets return-to-go at every MuJoCo segment while comparison numbers are imported from papers using standard protocols, weakening comparability.

T-Maze tests retention of only one bit and is heavily confounded by rare-action imbalance. The appendix shows that several recurrent baselines can achieve perfect extrapolation to 9,600 steps when trained on shorter sequences, undermining claims that RATE uniquely overcomes their memory limitations.

Reporting and reproducibility have material inconsistencies: POPGym is alternately described as containing 46 and 48 tasks; Table 2 calls apparent sums 'average' scores and gives no aggregate uncertainty; baseline hyperparameters and Atari/MuJoCo run counts are absent; initial memory is described as both learned and randomly sampled; and the equations, pseudocode, and hyperparameter table disagree about MRV's FFN and activation.

strengths: The manuscript addresses an important limitation of fixed-context trajectory transformers in partially observable, long-horizon offline RL, and motivates its segment-recurrent memory interface clearly. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/iclr2026--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-liua3g4w/call-35d3d79765cf4a849cef40e6008acc86/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}
The evaluation is broad, spanning several controlled memory tasks, POPGym, Atari, and MuJoCo, with transformer, recurrent, state-space, behavior-cloning, and offline-RL baselines.
The T-Maze length grid and ViZDoom cue-removal/window-split experiments provide useful evidence that RATE can exploit information beyond its local attention window.
The paper includes MRV variants, memory-corruption and segmentation ablations, multiple-run reporting, and practical measurements of parameters, runtime, and GPU memory.
weaknesses: The central preservation theorem is invalid. The proof selects j* because its attention weight is at least 1/m and then assumes it is the value row guaranteed to be alpha-aligned; these indices need not coincide. It also drops potentially negative terms from the attention-weighted sum and assumes the updated memory rows are unit-normalized, although the model does not enforce this. Moreover, the claimed preserved fraction is nonpositive for m>=2 and alpha<=1, including every reported configuration, making the lower bound vacuous.

The architectural novelty is limited: memory tokens largely follow RMT, hidden-state caching follows Transformer-XL, and MRV is a cross-attention update. The paper lacks a clean, trained-from-scratch factorial ablation of all three mechanisms across representative tasks; inference-time noise corruption cannot establish each component's contribution.

The MuJoCo comparison is not protocol-compatible. RATE resets the desired return-to-go to its maximum at every segment, whereas the reported competitors use results from their original standard protocols. Consequently, claims such as outperforming DT on all nine tasks are not supported by a controlled comparison.

The claimed unified architecture is heavily task-dependent: cached states are disabled for T-Maze, MRV is disabled for Memory Maze, the feed-forward block is selectively removed, and memory settings vary substantially. Comparable tuning budgets and full configurations are not reported for the baselines or for most POPGym tasks.

Several conclusions are overstated. RATE is not best on average in MuJoCo, Atari covers only four games, the Memory Maze advantage overlaps reported uncertainty, and POPGym's aggregate advantage over BC-LSTM is small and given without uncertainty. Thus the evidence does not establish a general-purpose state of the art.

Reporting contains consequential inconsistencies: POPGym is alternately described as containing 46 and 48 tasks; values called average normalized scores appear to be sums; the hierarchy used to calculate SEM across runs and episodes is unclear; and no statistical tests support repeated claims of significant improvement.

Reproducibility remains incomplete despite the appendix. Equation 3 and Algorithm 2 disagree about an FFN in MRV; the assumed memory normalization is absent; initialization versus learnability of M0 and gradient flow across segments are unclear; actual random seeds and detailed adapted-baseline configurations are not supplied.

Much of the strongest extrapolation evidence comes from T-Maze and AAR, which require retaining only one bit and provide an explicit junction flag. Per-grid results are also missing for the claimed 501x501 MiniGrid extrapolation. Richer long-horizon tests are needed to show that the method stores structured memories rather than merely preserves a binary cue.

strengths: The paper addresses an important problem: scalable long-horizon memory for offline reinforcement learning. RATE is conceptually understandable and combines segment recurrence, memory tokens, cached hidden states, and a selective update module.

The empirical scope is broad, covering several memory-oriented environments plus POPGym, Atari, and MuJoCo. Cue-removal tests, very-long-horizon extrapolation, memory-corruption diagnostics, architectural ablations, and efficiency measurements are valuable.

Some results are genuinely promising, particularly the ViZDoom performance and balance, T-Maze extrapolation to 9,600 steps, and reduced memory consumption relative to a full-context Decision Transformer.
The appendix documents environments, datasets, RATE hyperparameters, encoders, evaluation episode counts, and computational measurements.
weaknesses: Theorem 1 is invalid. The alignment assumption provides an aligned value row for each incoming memory row, while the pigeonhole argument provides a potentially different row receiving attention mass at least 1/m. The proof incorrectly identifies these rows and also ignores potentially negative contributions from all other value rows, so Equation 5 and both claimed bounds do not follow.

Even if repaired, the theorem would not substantiate the advertised guarantee. It omits the actual multi-head/FFN MRV, assumes normalization that the architecture does not enforce, and never verifies the claimed empirical alignment condition. Moreover, for the actual memory sizes m=5–30, the stated lower-bound coefficient is non-positive even at alpha=1, making the claimed preserved fraction vacuous.

The architectural novelty is incremental relative to RMT and Transformer-XL: the main addition is a cross-attention memory update. Direct comparisons against highly relevant memory methods discussed by the paper itself, including FFM, SHM, GTrXL, AGaLiTe, and RA-DT, are missing from the principal memory benchmarks.

The component evidence is incomplete. Corrupting a trained model at inference establishes reliance but not the benefit of each component during learning; there is no full retrained factorial ablation. Different headline experiments disable cached states or even MRV, weakening the claim that the three mechanisms jointly explain RATE's gains.

Several conclusions are overstated. The T-Maze heatmaps show that suitably short-trained BC-LSTM models can extrapolate strongly; RATE's Memory Maze advantage is small relative to reported uncertainty; Atari covers only four games; and RATE's average MuJoCo score trails several compared methods. Cross-paper standard-benchmark comparisons are also less controlled than same-code comparisons.

Reporting and reproducibility have notable gaps: POPGym is inconsistently described as containing 46 or 48 tasks, its reported 'average' aggregates appear to be sums, baseline hyperparameters and tuning budgets are largely absent, and run/seed counts are omitted for Atari and MuJoCo. The method specification is also inconsistent about whether MRV contains an FFN, while the hidden-state cache is absent from the pseudocode.
