strengths: The paper addresses an important problem and presents an intuitive architecture: recurrent segmentation, read/write memory tokens, cached hidden states, and the Memory Retention Valve provide a plausible route beyond Decision Transformer's fixed context. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/iclr2026--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-rwn2cg7j/call-5e65893091ad4434a441c641211e4e1d/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}
The empirical scope is unusually broad, covering synthetic memory diagnostics, image-based POMDPs, POPGym, Atari, and MuJoCo. The long-horizon T-Maze results and the MRV-CA-2 ablation are promising.

The paper includes useful implementation material: pseudocode, task descriptions, RATE hyperparameters, encoder configurations, run/episode counts for memory tasks, hardware information, and an efficiency comparison with DT.
The presentation is generally clear, with helpful architectural diagrams and attention visualizations, and the work raises no evident ethical concerns.
weaknesses: Theorem 1 is mathematically invalid. The alignment assumption guarantees an aligned value row exists, while the pigeonhole argument identifies a possibly different row receiving attention at least 1/m; the proof incorrectly treats these as the same row and also ignores potentially negative contributions from all other value rows. It additionally assumes normalization of the updated memory although the MRV does not enforce it.

Even under stronger assumptions, the stated preservation result would not justify the claim. For the actual settings with at least five memory tokens, 1-sqrt(2(1-alpha/m)) is negative and hence the lower bound is vacuous. Preserving Frobenius norm is not preserving information, the claimed empirical alpha-alignment is never measured, and a one-update statement gives no long-horizon guarantee.

The architectural novelty is modest relative to RMT, Transformer-XL, and standard cross-attention. Comparisons omit particularly relevant modern memory agents such as FFM and SHM, and baseline hyperparameters, capacities, and tuning budgets are not sufficiently documented to establish fairness.

The component evidence is incomplete. Injecting noise at inference is an out-of-distribution perturbation rather than a train-time removal ablation, so it does not isolate the benefits of memory tokens or cached states. MRV is convincingly ablated only on the synthetic one-bit T-Maze task, while the so-called OracleDT is a privileged-information reference rather than a valid performance upper bound.

There are material protocol inconsistencies. ViZDoom is described as containing 90-step trajectories with the pillar disappearing at step 45, yet a headline experiment trains on 150 steps and states that the pillar disappears at step 90. POPGym alternates between 46 and 48 tasks, baseline context settings are unspecified, and Table 2's values appear to be sums of per-task returns despite being described as averages.

Several empirical claims exceed the evidence. The strongest extrapolation result is essentially long-delay one-bit recall using all-successful oracle trajectories. On Memory Maze, RATE's advantage over RMT and TrXL is within the reported SEM; on POPGym its aggregate advantage over BC-LSTM is very small and lacks aggregate uncertainty; and Minigrid results are collapsed across grid sizes without per-size statistical comparisons.

The general-purpose offline-RL claim is not established. Atari covers only four games, while MuJoCo and Atari comparisons largely reuse numbers from other papers without complete seed information. MuJoCo also uses a RATE-specific return-to-go reset protocol without a matched ablation, and RATE's average MuJoCo score is below several reported competitors. These issues, together with the invalid central theory, place the paper below the acceptance threshold.

strengths: The paper addresses an important problem: retaining information beyond a transformer's fixed context in partially observable offline RL. The read/write memory-token construction and segment-level recurrence are intuitive and practically motivated.

The empirical scope is unusually broad, covering several dedicated memory environments, all 48 reported POPGym variants, and standard Atari and MuJoCo tasks. RATE shows particularly promising robustness on long T-Maze sequences and strong results on ViZDoom-Two-Colors.

The paper includes useful diagnostics and ablations over MRV variants, memory corruption, segmentation, transformer size, and computational cost. Environment descriptions, primary hyperparameters, run counts, and hardware are also provided.

The manuscript is generally well organized and visually legible, with helpful architectural diagrams and extensive appendices. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/iclr2026--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-6xxwpczk/call-406fbcffa31a4f0d87282f46c6520157/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}
weaknesses: Theorem 1 is incorrect. The proof separately establishes that some attention weight is at least 1/m and that some value vector is alpha-aligned, then unjustifiably treats these as the same index. It also drops potentially negative contributions from other value vectors and assumes the updated memory row is unit-normalized although neither the theorem nor architecture ensures this. Simple counterexamples therefore violate the claimed bound.

Even setting aside the invalid proof, the advertised lower bound is vacuous for the actual configurations: with alpha<=1 and m>=5 memory tokens, 1-sqrt(2(1-alpha/m)) is negative. A norm lower bound would also not establish preservation of task-relevant information, and a one-step result would not guarantee retention across thousands of recurrent updates. The claimed empirical alpha-alignment is not measured.

The T-Maze evidence does not cleanly isolate long-term memory. The task has extreme action imbalance, which the appendix itself acknowledges, yet no class-balanced loss or decision-step oversampling baseline is tested. Appendix results show that DGRU and some LSTM configurations can generalize perfectly to 9,600 steps when trained on shorter sequences, contradicting broad statements that recurrent models cannot retain such information.

Several central comparisons are incomplete or confounded. POPGym excludes the paper's own RMT, Transformer-XL, and Decision Mamba baselines as well as relevant memory-specific methods such as FFM and SHM. MuJoCo uses a RATE-specific reset of return-to-go at every segment, without applying or ablating this change for DT, while most comparator numbers are imported from other papers. Atari covers only four games, and run counts for Atari and MuJoCo are omitted.

The component evidence is weaker than claimed. Replacing memory or cached states with random noise at inference creates an out-of-distribution perturbation rather than a controlled architectural ablation. A full factorial comparison of memory tokens, hidden-state caching, and MRV trained from scratch is absent, and the only substantive MRV removal study is on T-Maze.

Important implementation details remain unclear despite the reproducibility claim. The core hidden-state cache is absent from Algorithm 1 and the mathematical definition; initialization is described as Gaussian despite calling the memory embeddings learned; Equation 3 includes an FFN omitted by Algorithm 2; and positional encodings, inference return conditioning, gradient flow, baseline hyperparameters, and task-specific POPGym configurations are not adequately specified.

Reporting contains consequential inconsistencies and overclaims. The POPGym value 9.53 is the sum over 48 tasks, not the stated average (the mean is about 0.199); the memory-subset value 0.45 likewise corresponds to only about 0.014 per task. The manuscript alternates between 46 and 48 POPGym tasks, and claims broad superiority despite RATE averaging below several methods on MuJoCo and showing only small or statistically unresolved gains on some memory benchmarks.

Novelty is moderate: RATE mainly combines RMT-style memory tokens, Transformer-XL caching, and a standard cross-attention update. Given the invalid theoretical justification and missing comparisons against closely related memory architectures, the evidence is insufficient for acceptance at a selective top-tier venue.

strengths: Addresses an important problem in offline RL: retaining sparse information beyond a transformer's fixed context. The recurrent segmentation design is intuitive and practically relevant.
Evaluates across diverse modalities and environments, with particularly striking extrapolation results on T-Maze up to 9,600 steps.
Provides useful ablations of MRV variants, memory corruption, segment configurations, transformer hyperparameters, and computational efficiency.
The manuscript is generally well organized and reports per-task RATE hyperparameters, run counts, seed counts, and implementation resources.
weaknesses: Theorem 1 is incorrect. The aligned value row need not be the row receiving attention weight at least 1/m; other value rows may contribute negative inner products; and the proof assumes the MRV output is normalized without establishing this. Moreover, the claimed preservation factor is non-positive for the usual m >= 2 settings, making the lower bound vacuous even if the derivation were valid. This invalidates a prominent theoretical claim.

The architectural novelty is limited: RATE combines RMT-style memory tokens, Transformer-XL caching, and standard cross-attention. The paper does not compare adequately against several closely relevant modern memory mechanisms, such as FFM and SHM.

Some comparisons are not controlled. MuJoCo results use a nonstandard return-to-go reset specifically for RATE while many baseline numbers are copied from prior papers. RATE's average is below several reported methods, contradicting the broad claim that it matches or outperforms specialized algorithms.

The main component evidence is incomplete. Inference-time replacement with noise creates an out-of-distribution perturbation and does not substitute for training clean variants without memory tokens or caching. Strong factorial ablations across the main environments are missing.

Statistical support is weak for claims of significant and consistent improvement: most experiments use only three to six training runs, no hypothesis tests are reported, and several gains have overlapping error bars.

POPGym reporting is internally inconsistent about evaluating 46 versus 48 tasks. The aggregate values appear to be sums of heterogeneous task returns despite being described as average normalized scores, and comparisons omit strong recurrent, state-space, and memory-transformer baselines.

The headline generalization evidence relies heavily on synthetic one-bit recall tasks with oracle-generated successful demonstrations. Results on richer tasks are less decisive, while exact baseline hyperparameters, tuning budgets, and several recurrence/training details are insufficiently documented.

strengths: The manuscript is readable and visually well organized, with useful architecture diagrams and a substantial appendix :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/iclr2026--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-a2bb7diy/call-b817510f25074947886b9d9282d20ddc/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}.
The long-horizon memory problem is important, and combining recurrent memory tokens, cached states, and selective updates is practically motivated.
The evaluation spans several modalities and benchmarks. RATE shows notable empirical performance on ViZDoom, Memory Maze, and especially T-Maze extrapolation far beyond its training horizon.
The paper reports dataset construction, many hyperparameters, multiple runs for the memory experiments, component analyses, and useful compute and GPU-memory measurements.
weaknesses: Theorem 1 is incorrect. The proof selects an index with attention weight at least 1/m and then assumes it is the existentially aligned index, ignores potentially negative contributions from all other values, and uses normalization of the MRV output that the architecture does not enforce. Simple counterexamples violate the claimed bound.

Even overlooking the invalid proof, the theorem does not establish useful memory retention: its alpha-alignment premise essentially assumes the desired property without empirical verification, and the stated lower bound is nonpositive for the numbers of memory tokens used in the experiments. Preserving vector norm also does not imply preserving task-relevant information.

The architectural novelty is limited: most of RATE consists of established RMT-style memory tokens and Transformer-XL caching, with a relatively simple cross-attention postprocessor. The experiments do not cleanly establish the incremental value of all three components; inference-time noise is not a substitute for training each ablated architecture, and the MRV comparison is concentrated on the synthetic T-Maze task.

Several comparisons are confounded or incomplete. Atari and MuJoCo results are partly imported from prior papers, run counts are not reported, only four Atari games are tested, and RATE uses a nonstandard segment-wise return reset on MuJoCo without reevaluating DT under the same strategy. Strong recent memory methods discussed in related work are also absent from the main memory benchmarks.

The POPGym presentation is misleading and inconsistent. The paper alternates between 46 and 48 tasks, and the reported overall score of 9.5 is a sum of 48 per-task returns rather than an average; the actual mean is about 0.199 versus 0.187 for BC-LSTM. This small aggregate advantage is unsupported by paired significance analysis, and RATE loses on many individual tasks.

Important implementation details are internally inconsistent or omitted: the main algorithm does not specify the claimed hidden-state cache, Equation 3 includes an FFN whereas Algorithm 2 does not, memory initialization and gradient flow across segments are unclear, and baseline architectures and tuning budgets are insufficiently documented.

Claims of significant, consistent, state-of-the-art, and general-purpose superiority are stronger than the evidence. Several gains are within reported uncertainty, no statistical tests are provided, the most dramatic extrapolation evidence comes from one-bit recall tasks, and RATE is not best on the average MuJoCo score. These issues, together with the false central theorem, place the paper clearly below the acceptance threshold.

strengths: The paper addresses an important problem: retaining sparse information beyond a transformer's context window in offline partially observable RL.
RATE is a coherent hybrid of recurrent memory tokens, cached hidden states, and a cross-attention memory update. The T-Maze results provide meaningful evidence of long-context extrapolation.
The evaluation spans several memory-oriented environments and standard control benchmarks, with comparisons to transformer, recurrent, state-space, behavior-cloning, and offline-RL baselines.
The MRV-variant and segmentation ablations show a substantial empirical advantage for the selected configuration on T-Maze.
The appendix reports run counts, many RATE hyperparameters, parameter counts, latency, and memory consumption, and the presentation is generally polished.
weaknesses: Theorem 1 and its proof are invalid. The assumption only states that some value row is aligned with each incoming memory row, but the proof incorrectly assumes that this is the row receiving attention weight at least 1/m. It also discards potentially negative contributions from other value rows and treats the MRV output as unit-normalized without assuming or proving this. Moreover, for the practical m>1 settings, the stated norm lower bound is generally negative and therefore vacuous. Thus, the claimed theoretical memory-preservation guarantee is unsupported.

The architectural novelty is limited: RATE largely combines RMT-style memory tokens and Transformer-XL caching, while MRV-CA-2 is ordinary cross-attention from old to updated memory without an explicit gate or residual preservation path. Comparisons to closely relevant modern memory agents such as FFM and SHM are absent despite their discussion in related work.

The central implementation is underspecified and internally inconsistent. Hidden-state caching does not appear in Algorithm 1, memory is described both as learned and as sampled from N(0,1), and Equation 3 includes an FFN while Algorithm 2 omits it and the reported MRV activation. Gradient flow across recurrent segments and cache handling during long inference are also unclear.

The component evidence is incomplete. The main RQ1 experiment corrupts trained representations with out-of-distribution noise at inference, which predictably damages a network but does not establish that each component improves learning. A controlled training-time ablation of memory tokens, caching, and MRV is missing.

Several broad claims exceed the results. RATE's Memory Maze advantage overlaps the reported uncertainty; Minigrid reports only an aggregate box plot rather than per-grid extrapolation results; at 9600-step T-Maze inference RATE is around 0.72 and is not clearly better than some recurrent baselines; and its MuJoCo average of 78.5 is below the reported 83.2 best baseline.

The POPGym reporting is problematic: the manuscript alternates between 46 and 48 tasks, while the stated 33+15 split and Table 9 contain 48. Table 2 calls values such as 9.5 'average normalized scores,' although they appear to be sums of per-task scores bounded near [-1,1]. The aggregate advantage over BC-LSTM is small, has no uncertainty or statistical test, and does not justify the claimed consistent failure of alternatives.

Important protocol inconsistencies undermine confidence. ViZDoom is described as having 5,000 trajectories of length 90, yet a central experiment trains on length 150; the cue is variously said to disappear at steps 45 and 90; and RMT's reported imbalance is lower than RATE's despite the claim that RATE is lowest. Atari/MuJoCo run counts are omitted, several results are imported from other papers, and RATE uses a special segment-wise return reset on MuJoCo, making the comparison difficult to interpret.

Overall, there is promising empirical evidence, but the false theorem, incremental contribution, incomplete method specification, and multiple evaluation/reporting issues prevent the work from meeting the technical-soundness and evidence standards of a top-tier venue.

strengths: The manuscript :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/iclr2026--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-pm1n40w4/call-4876bd0299be42b080f31cbfdb056f54/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"} addresses an important problem and presents a clear segment-recurrent architecture combining memory tokens, cached states, and a cross-attention memory update.

The evaluation is broad, spanning several memory-focused environments, POPGym, Atari, and MuJoCo. The long-horizon T-Maze extrapolation is particularly compelling, and the paper reports multiple runs and uncertainty for the principal memory experiments.

The appendices provide useful environment descriptions, RATE hyperparameters, architectural ablations, and efficiency measurements; the reported memory savings relative to a full-context Decision Transformer are practically relevant.
weaknesses: Theorem 1 is incorrect. The proof conflates the index receiving attention mass at least 1/m with the potentially different index guaranteed to be alpha-aligned; it also drops possibly negative contributions from other values and assumes the MRV output is unit-normalized without justification. Moreover, for the employed m greater than or equal to 2, the claimed preservation lower bound is non-positive and therefore vacuous. This invalidates a prominently stated theoretical contribution.

The novelty is limited: RATE largely combines RMT-style read/write tokens with Transformer-XL caching, while the main new element is a simple cross-attention operation. The paper does not adequately distinguish this operation from existing memory-update mechanisms or compare empirically against several relevant memory architectures discussed in related work.

The evidence is substantially weaker than the claims of consistent or significant superiority. Memory Maze confidence intervals overlap with RMT and TrXL, POPGym is nearly tied with BC-LSTM, and no significance tests are reported. POPGym totals are called averages despite appearing to be sums, the paper inconsistently reports 46 versus 48 tasks, and Figure 4 contradicts the claim that RATE has the lowest imbalance because RMT is slightly lower.

Several comparisons are not controlled. The POPGym study omits RMT, TrXL, Mamba, FFM, and SHM; Atari and MuJoCo results are compared partly with numbers from other papers; RATE uses a longer effective history; and MuJoCo introduces a favorable segment-wise reset of the target return that is not used by the cited baselines. RATE is also not best overall on either standard benchmark.

The component evidence is incomplete: replacing trained memories with noise at inference only shows that the model depends on them, not that each proposed mechanism improves learning. There is no clean train-time factorial ablation of memory tokens, caching, and MRV. Cached-state handling is absent from the main algorithm, baseline configurations and tuning budgets are not documented, and the MRV equations, pseudocode, and activation description are inconsistent. Taken together with the false theorem, these issues put the work clearly below the acceptance threshold despite promising empirical results.

strengths: The paper targets an important problem—long-horizon memory in offline RL—and presents an intuitive segment-recurrent transformer combining memory tokens, cached hidden states, and a cross-attention memory update.

The empirical scope is unusually broad, covering several synthetic and visual memory tasks, POPGym, Atari, and MuJoCo. RATE shows particularly promising results on ViZDoom and long-horizon T-Maze evaluations.
The authors compare against transformer, recurrent, MLP, and state-space baselines and report multiple training runs and evaluation seeds for the principal memory experiments.
The MRV-variant study, memory-corruption diagnostics, architectural sweeps, hyperparameter tables, and computational measurements provide useful empirical insight beyond headline results.
weaknesses: Theorem 1 is invalid under its stated assumptions. The proof conflates the value vector guaranteed to be aligned with the index receiving attention weight at least 1/m; these indices need not coincide. It also drops potentially negative contributions from all other values and assumes normalization of the updated memory without establishing it. Moreover, for the employed m>2, the claimed preservation coefficient is negative and hence vacuous. Thus, the paper's theoretical memory-preservation claim is unsupported.

The architectural novelty is limited: RATE largely combines RMT-style memory tokens, Transformer-XL caching, and a relatively direct cross-attention update. There is no retrained factorial ablation isolating all three advertised mechanisms, and evidence specifically supporting MRV is concentrated on the one-bit T-Maze task; inference-time noising is not a substitute for training models without each component.

The headline 9,600-step evaluation is a highly structured one-bit retention problem with oracle demonstrations and an explicit pre-junction flag. Appendix results show that DGRU and sometimes other recurrent baselines can also extrapolate perfectly when trained at favorable shorter horizons, weakening the claim that this result uniquely demonstrates RATE's long-term-memory advantage.

Baseline coverage and fairness are uneven. POPGym omits especially relevant memory architectures such as RMT, Transformer-XL, FFM, and SHM. Atari and MuJoCo comparisons import results from other papers, while RATE uses longer recurrent effective contexts and, for MuJoCo, a custom procedure that resets return-to-go to its maximum at every segment. These comparisons do not convincingly establish a general-purpose state of the art.

Several conclusions exceed the evidence. RATE's MuJoCo average is 78.5 versus 83.2 for a Decision Mamba variant, Memory Maze improvements have overlapping SEMs, and the POPGym aggregate advantage over BC-LSTM is small. No statistical tests support repeated claims of significant improvement.

Experimental reporting contains material inconsistencies: POPGym is alternately described as having 46 and 48 tasks; its bounded per-task normalized returns are summed in Table 2 but repeatedly called averages; and uncertainty aggregation over training runs versus evaluation episodes is unclear. The Minigrid box plot also collapses all grid sizes, obscuring where extrapolation succeeds or fails.

Reproducibility is incomplete despite the extensive appendix. The algorithms do not specify how cached states enter each layer, positional treatment across segments, gradient truncation, or precise causal action-prediction alignment. Equation 3 includes an FFN absent from Algorithm 2, and baseline hyperparameters, selection procedures, and complete per-task POPGym settings are not reported.

strengths: RATE is clearly motivated and presented, combining recurrent memory tokens, cached hidden states, and a cross-attention Memory Retention Valve in a coherent architecture. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/iclr2026--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-x0yuaq5x/call-7bc6e72288404df8857b7ea6655e0652/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}
The empirical scope is broad, covering several memory-intensive domains, very long T-Maze extrapolation, POPGym, Atari, and MuJoCo, with transformer, recurrent, state-space, and offline-RL baselines.
Results on T-Maze and ViZDoom provide promising evidence that RATE retains sparse cues beyond a standard transformer's context window; the comparison among several MRV variants is also informative.
The appendices report architecture settings, encoders, run counts, computational measurements, and many additional ablations, while code availability supports reproducibility.
weaknesses: Theorem 1 and its proof are invalid. The aligned value row need not be the attention row having weight at least 1/m; other value rows may contribute negative inner products; the proof assumes the output memory rows are normalized although the defined MRV does not normalize them; and it omits the actual multi-head/FFN transformation. Moreover, the claimed preservation lower bound is non-positive for the typical setting m>=2, making it vacuous even if derived correctly. This directly undermines the paper's main theoretical claim.

The component evidence is incomplete: much of RQ1 corrupts inputs only at inference instead of retraining principled variants without memory tokens or cached states. Major components are also disabled in some headline experiments, yet the paper presents RATE as one unified three-component architecture.

Baseline coverage is uneven. POPGym—the broadest memory benchmark—compares only against DT, BC-LSTM, BC-MLP, and random, omitting the most relevant memory-transformer and modern memory-agent baselines discussed in related work. The novelty otherwise appears incremental over RMT-style tokens, Transformer-XL caching, and a straightforward cross-attention update.

The standard-benchmark comparisons are not fully controlled. MuJoCo resets return-to-go to its maximum at every segment, changing the conditioning protocol, while competing scores are imported from papers using the conventional protocol. RATE's overall MuJoCo average is also below several reported methods, so the general-purpose and state-of-the-art language is overstated.

Statistical support is weak for several claimed improvements: most experiments use only three to six training runs, no hypothesis tests or confidence intervals are supplied, and some leading results have overlapping SEMs. The aggregated Minigrid plot also does not substantiate the claim of consistently strong performance at every tested grid size.

There are material reporting and reproducibility inconsistencies: POPGym alternates between 46 and 48 tasks; its purported average normalized scores appear to be sums; ViZDoom descriptions conflict over when the pillar disappears and how 150-step training data are obtained from a stated 90-step dataset; baseline tuning details and standard-benchmark run counts are missing; and the pseudocode does not specify hidden-state caching or whether the initial memory is random or learned.
